day01-pronunciation.title: Day 1: Pronunciation & First Greetings

vocab.notes: Present tense of "to be" for things and states. alt: cha

day01-pronunciation.notes_markdown:
## Notes
Nepali has aspirated and unaspirated consonant pairs that English does not
distinguish. Getting these wrong changes the word, so drill them on day 1:

- **क ka** vs **ख kha** - the second has a puff of air after it.
- **त ta** vs **थ tha** - the tongue touches the teeth, not the ridge behind them.
- **ट ṭa** vs **त ta** - the retroflex ट curls the tongue back. This is the
  contrast English speakers find hardest.

Nepali is subject-object-verb. The verb lands at the end of the sentence, so
"I eat rice" comes out as "I rice eat".

day02-survival-phrases.title: Day 2: Survival Phrases

spans.english: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
It is over there on the right.

day02-survival-phrases.notes_markdown:
## Notes
These are the phrases that keep you afloat before you can build sentences of
your own. Learn them as whole units — don't try to break them down grammatically
yet. The grammar comes in the Day 4 and Day 5 templates; right now the goal is to
be able to *say something* in any situation.

Politeness is not optional in Nepali. Almost every request takes the `-नुहोस्`
(`-nuhos`) ending, which is the polite imperative — `दिनुहोस्` "please give",
`भन्नुहोस्` "please say", `बोल्नुहोस्` "please speak". Drop it and you sound
rude, not casual.

Two survival reflexes to over-learn:

- **बुझिनँ** (`bujhina`) — "I didn't understand." Say it early and often.
- **बिस्तारै भन्नुहोस्** (`bistarai bhannuhos`) — "Please say it slowly."

`माफ गर्नुहोस्` opens almost any interaction with a stranger — it covers both
"excuse me" (to get attention) and "sorry" (to apologise).

day03-core-words.title: Day 3: First 100 Core Words

examples.english: Today I go to the market

spans.english: How many people are in your house?

spans.devanagari: आमा, बुबा, दाइ, बहिनी र म।
spans.romanized: Aama, buba, dai, bahini ra ma.
spans.english: Mother, father, older brother, younger sister, and me.

day03-core-words.notes_markdown:
## Notes
This is a pure vocabulary day. The words here are the ones that show up in
almost every sentence you will ever say: family members, everyday food, common
places, and the words for "today / tomorrow / yesterday / now". Learn them as
flashcards first, then come back and read the dialogue.

A few notes on the words:

- **आमा / बुबा** are "mother / father" as address terms too — you call your own
  parents this directly.
- Older and younger siblings have different words: **दाइ / दिदी** (older
  brother / sister) vs **भाइ / बहिनी** (younger). Nepali speakers also use
  दाइ / दिदी for slightly older strangers as a politeness.
- **भात** is cooked rice on the plate; **चामल** is uncooked rice in the sack.
  Different words, and mixing them up is a classic beginner tell.
- The verb still lands at the end: "I eat rice today" → *म आज भात खान्छु*
  (I today rice eat).

day04-sentence-patterns.title: Day 4: The Core Sentence Templates

spans.devanagari: हजुर, मलाई चिया धेरै मन पर्छ।
spans.romanized: Hajur, malai chiya dherai man parchha.
spans.english: Yes, I like tea very much.

day04-sentence-patterns.notes_markdown:
## Notes
These are the highest-leverage templates in the whole course. Each one generates
hundreds of sentences once you can swap the slot freely. Drill the slot, not the
sentence: say ten different things with the same frame before moving on.

The `___` marker is what the fill-in-the-blank game reads, so keep it exactly
three underscores.

day05-sentence-drills.title: Day 5: Sentence Drills

examples.english: I get up in the morning

spans.english: What time do you get up in the morning?
What do you do after that?
In the evening I come home.
What do you do at night?

spans.devanagari: म खाना खान्छु र किताब पढ्छु।
spans.romanized: Ma khana khanchhu ra kitab padhchhu.
spans.english: I eat food and read a book.

day05-sentence-drills.notes_markdown:
## Notes
Day 4 gave you the "I am / I like / I need / I want" frames. Today is about
verbs and the **present habitual** tense — the one you use for "I eat rice",
"I go to work", "I get up early".

The pattern for regular verbs, first person:

- Take the dictionary form: **खानु** (`khanu`, "to eat")
- Drop `-नु`, add `-न्छु`: **खान्छु** (`khanchhu`, "I eat")

Polite second person swaps in `-नुहुन्छ`: **तपाईं खानुहुन्छ** (`tapai
khanuhunchha`, "you eat"). Third person is `-न्छ` / `-न्छिन्` (he / she).

Two things to drill hard:

1. **Word order.** Object before verb, always. "I drink tea" = *म चिया
   पिउँछु* (I tea drink).
2. **The `-न` infinitive** for "to be able to" and "want to": *म पढ्न सक्छु*
   (I read-can), *म जान चाहन्छु* (I go-want).

day06-questions.title: Day 6: Asking Questions
day06-questions.notes_markdown:
## Notes
Nepali question words all start with **क** (`k`), which makes them easy to
group: के / को / कहाँ / कहिले / किन / कसरी / कति / कुन / कस्तो.

Two rules make questions much easier than they look:

1. **Word order does not change.** A statement becomes a question by swapping in
   a question word where the answer would go: *यो राम्रो छ* ("this is good") →
   *यो कस्तो छ?* ("how is this?").
2. **Yes/no questions** just add a rising tone, or the particle **नि** or a
   question mark in writing. *तपाईंलाई चिया मन पर्छ* → *तपाईंलाई चिया मन पर्छ?*

The verb still comes last, so the question word usually sits in the middle, not
the front: *तपाईंको नाम **के** हो?* not "*के तपाईंको नाम हो?*".

day07-week1-review.title: Day 7: Week 1 Review

spans.romanized: Hajur, malai dal bhat dherai man parchha.

You'll get used to it slowly.

spans.english: How many days will you stay in Nepal?

spans.english: So I study Nepali every day.

day07-week1-review.notes_markdown:
## Notes
No new grammar today. This is a consolidation day: the dialogue below reuses
every pattern from Week 1 in one connected conversation — a first meeting between
a Nepali speaker and a foreign learner.

Work it in three passes:

1. Listen with all three lines visible.
2. Hide the English and shadow each line aloud.
3. Cover Ram's lines and try to produce them yourself before revealing.

The only new words are the connectives — **अनि, तर, किनभने, त्यसैले, पनि** —
which are what turn a list of sentences into actual speech. Drill those.

Week 1 self-check — you should be able to, without looking:

- Greet someone and give your name and country
- Ask and answer "how are you" and "what's your name"
- Ask where something is and how much it costs
- Say what you like, need, and want
- Say what you do in a normal day

day09-directions.title: Day 9: Asking for Directions

examples.english: How far is it from here?

spans.english: Excuse me, which way is Thamel?

spans.devanagari: सिधा जानुहोस्, अनि पहिलो चोकमा दायाँ मोड्नुहोस्।
spans.romanized: Sidha januhos, ani pahilo chokma dayan modnuhos.
spans.english: Go straight, then turn right at the first intersection.
You'll get there in ten minutes.
Straight, then right at the first intersection.

day09-directions.notes_markdown:
## Notes
Directions in Nepali lean on a small set of position words plus the postposition
**-तिर** (`-tira`, "towards"): *दायाँतिर* "to the right", *बायाँतिर* "to the
left", *सिधा* "straight".

The key verbs:

- **जानु** (`janu`) "to go" — *सिधा जानुहोस्* "go straight"
- **मोड्नु** (`modnu`) "to turn" — *दायाँ मोड्नुहोस्* "turn right"
- **पुग्नु** (`pugnu`) "to arrive / reach" — *कति बेरमा पुगिन्छ?* "how long to
  get there?"

Landmarks take the postposition **-को छेउमा** ("next to") or **-को अगाडि** ("in
front of"): *मन्दिरको छेउमा* "next to the temple".

When someone gives you directions fast, fall back to Day 2: *बिस्तारै
भन्नुहोस्* and *फेरि भन्नुहोस्*.

day10-shopping.title: Day 10: Shopping and Prices

examples.english: How much is one kilo of potatoes?
I would like half a kilo of apples

spans.english: Sister, how much are tomatoes per kilo?
I can't go lower than that.

spans.devanagari: एक किलो दिनुहोस्, अनि एउटा झोला पनि।
spans.romanized: Ek kilo dinuhos, ani euta jhola pani.
spans.english: Give me one kilo, and a bag too.

day10-shopping.notes_markdown:
## Notes
This lesson pulls together numbers, prices, and polite bargaining. Nepali counts
in a base-ten system but the words are irregular up to about 40, so drill 1–20
plus the tens (बीस, तीस, चालीस, पचास...) as raw memorisation.

Prices use **रुपैयाँ** (`rupaiyan`). "Per kilo" is **किलोको** — the `-को`
genitive doing "of / per". "How much for all of it" is **जम्मा कति?**

Bargaining phrases you'll actually use:

- **अलि महँगो भयो** — "that's a bit expensive"
- **अलि घटाउनुहोस् न** — "lower it a little, please"
- **अन्तिम कति?** — "what's your final price?"

`न` on the end of a request softens it, like "…won't you?".

day11-family.title: Day 11: Family and Relationships

examples.english: My older sister is in Kathmandu

patterns.template_english: There are ___ people in my family

examples.english: There are four people in my family
There are six people in my family
There are five people in my family
What does your older brother do?

spans.english: How many people are in your family?
Father, mother, younger sister, and me.
My mother teaches at a school.
How old is your younger sister?

day11-family.notes_markdown:
## Notes
Nepali family terms are much more specific than English. Age and side of the
family both matter:

- Your father's younger brother is **काका**; his older brother is **ठूलो बुबा**.
- Your mother's brother is **मामा** (a completely different word).
- Older sibling vs younger sibling is never blurred: **दाइ / दिदी** vs
  **भाइ / बहिनी**.

For talking *about* family respectfully, use the honorific verb **हुनुहुन्छ**
instead of **छ**: *मेरो बुबा घरमा हुनुहुन्छ* ("my father is at home").

To say how many of something: number + counter. People take **जना**
(*तीन जना*, "three people"); things take **वटा** (*दुई वटा*, "two of them").

script-devanagari.title: Reference: The Devanagari Script

characters.notes: The inherent vowel carried by every bare consonant
Velar, aspirated - a puff of air
Written after the consonant: क + ा = का
Written BEFORE the consonant but pronounced after: क + ि = कि

script-devanagari.notes_markdown:
## Notes
This is the source for the character recognition drill. Two or three short
bursts a day gets you sounding out words within a few days. Do not spend weeks
on handwriting.

Two things to hold onto:

- Every consonant carries an inherent **a** sound. क alone is "ka", not "k".
- A vowel written **after** a consonant is a matra, a modified mark rather than
  the standalone letter. क + ि = कि "ki". Standalone इ only appears at the start
  of a word.

The retroflex row (ट ठ ड ढ ण) is pronounced with the tongue curled back against
the roof of the mouth. English has no equivalent, and confusing it with the
dental row (त थ द ध न) is the single most common beginner error.

week02-conversation-cafe.notes_markdown:
## Notes
This is the first dialogue long enough to drill as a response chain: read one
turn, then produce the next before revealing it. The two question forms here,
`के गर्दै हुनुहुन्छ?` and `कहाँ जाँदै हुनुहुन्छ?`, are worth over-learning.
They open more conversations than any other pair.
